arXiv:1910.07904v4 [math.AP] 16 Oct 2020

On the Cauchy problem of 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system

Xiaopeng Zhao Address: College of SciencesNortheastern UniversityShenyang 110819,    P. R. China Email address: zhaoxiaopeng@jiangnan.edu.cn
Abstract.

In this paper, we are concerned with the well-posedness and large time behavior of Cauchy problem for 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard equations. First, using Banach fixed point theorem, we establish the local well-posedness of solutions. Second, assuming ‖(u0,ϕ,∇ϕ0)‖H˙12\|(u_{0},\phi,\nabla\phi_{0})\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}} is sufficiently small, we obtain the global well-posedness of solutions in the critical space. Moreover, the optimal decay rates of the higher-order spatial derivatives of the solution are also obtained.

Key words and phrases: 
Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system, global well-posedness, decay, pure energy method.
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
35K55, 76D03, 76D05.

1. Introduction

In Fluid Mechanics, the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations models the motions of single-phase fluids such as oil or water. Sometimes, we also need to understand the motion of binary fluid mixtures, that is fluids composed by either two phases of the same chemical species or phases of different composition. Diffuse interface methods are widely used by many authors to describe the behavior of complex (e.g., binary) fluids [5, 12]. The Model H [23, 24, 30] is a diffuse interface model for incompressible isothermal two-phase flows. This model include the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations for the (averged) velocity uu nonlinearly coupled with a convective Cahn-Hilliard equation for the (relative) concentration difference φ\varphi.

Suppose that the temperature variations are negligible, taking the density is equal to 11, and let the viscosity ν\nu be constant, the Model H reduces to the incompressible Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system [2, 9, 25]

(1) {∂tu−νΔu+u⋅∇u+∇π=𝒦μ∇φ,div​u=0,∂tφ+u⋅∇φ=∇⋅(M∇μ),μ=−ε​Δ​φ+ζ​F′​(φ),\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}u-\nu\Delta u+u\cdot\nabla u+\nabla\pi=\mathcal{K}\mu\nabla\varphi,\\ &\hbox{div}u=0,\\ &\partial_{t}\varphi+u\cdot\nabla\varphi=\nabla\cdot(M\nabla\mu),\\ &\mu=-\varepsilon\Delta\varphi+\zeta F^{\prime}(\varphi),\end{aligned}\right.

in Ω×(0,∞)\Omega\times(0,\infty) with Ω⊆ℝ3\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{3} is a bounded domain or the whole space. In equations (1), uu denotes the mean velocity, π\pi represent the pressure and φ\varphi is an order parameter related to the concentration of the two fluids (e.g. the concentration difference or the concentration of one component), respectively. The quantities μ≥0\mu\geq 0, M≥0M\geq 0 and 𝒦≥0\mathcal{K}\geq 0 are positive constants that correspond to the kinematic viscosity of fluid, mobility constant and capillarity (stress) coefficient, respectively. Moreover, μ\mu denotes the chemical potential of the mixture which can be given by the variational derivative of the free energy functional

(2) ℱ⁡(φ)=∫Ω(ε2​|∇φ|2+ζ​F​(φ))​𝑑x.\mathcal{F}(\varphi)=\int_{\Omega}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}|\nabla\varphi|^{2}+\zeta F(\varphi)\right)dx.

Usually, we take F⁡(φ)=∫0φf⁡(ξ)​𝑑ξF(\varphi)=\int_{0}^{\varphi}f(\xi)d\xi as a double-well potential with two equal minima ±1\pm 1 corresponding to the two pure phases

(3) F⁡(s)=14​(s2−1)2,F(s)=\frac{1}{4}(s^{2}-1)^{2},

or a singular free energy

(4) F⁡(s)=θ2​[(1+s)​log⁡(1+s)+(1−s)​log⁡(1−s)]−θc2​s2,F(s)=\frac{\theta}{2}[(1+s)\log(1+s)+(1-s)\log(1-s)]-\frac{\theta_{c}}{2}s^{2},

where s∈[−1,1]s\in[-1,1] and 0<θ<θc0<\theta<\theta_{c}.

Remark 1.1.

In [18], the authors pointed out that

𝒦μ∇φ=𝒦∇(ε2|∇φ|2+ξF(φ))−𝒦∇⋅(∇φ⊗∇φ).\mathcal{K}\mu\nabla\varphi=\mathcal{K}\nabla\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}|\nabla\varphi|^{2}+\xi F(\varphi)\right)-\mathcal{K}\nabla\cdot(\nabla\varphi\otimes\nabla\varphi).

Moreover, the notation ∇φ⊗∇φ\nabla\varphi\otimes\nabla\varphi denotes the 3×33\times 3 matrix whose (i,j)(i,j)th entry is given by ∂iφ⋅∂jφ\partial_{i}\varphi\cdot\partial_{j}\varphi, 1≤i,j≤31\leq i,j\leq 3, and hence

∇⋅(∇φ⊗∇φ)=Δ​φ⋅∇φ+12​∑k=13∇|∇φk|2.\nabla\cdot(\nabla\varphi\otimes\nabla\varphi)=\Delta\varphi\cdot\nabla\varphi+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{3}\nabla|\nabla\varphi_{k}|^{2}.

Therefore, (1)1 can be replaced by

∂tu+u⋅∇u−νΔu+∇π~=−𝒦Δφ⋅∇φ,\partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla u-\nu\Delta u+\nabla\tilde{\pi}=-\mathcal{K}\Delta\varphi\cdot\nabla\varphi,

with π~=π−𝒦⁡(ε2​|∇φ|2+ξ​F​(φ))+𝒦2​∑k=13∇|∇φk|2.\tilde{\pi}=\pi-\mathcal{K}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}|\nabla\varphi|^{2}+\xi F(\varphi)\right)+\frac{\mathcal{K}}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{3}\nabla|\nabla\varphi_{k}|^{2}.

In a sense, the incompressible Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard equation can be seen as the coupling between the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with the convective Cahn-Hilliard equations. This coupling of equations was highly studied from the theoretical and mathematical point of view. Till now, there is a large amount of literature on the mathematical analysis of initial-boundary value problem for Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system in 2D or 3D case. Abels et. al. [1, 3, 4], Boyer [7], Eleuteri, Rocca and Schimperna [13], Gal, Grasselli and Miranville [19], Lam and Wu [28] studied the existence of global weak solution and unique strong solution for Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system with non-constant mobility; Gal and Grasselli [18] considered the asymptotic behavior of 2D Navier-Stokes-Navier-Stokes system, proved the existence of global attractor and exponential attractor; Colli, Frigeri and Grasselli [11], Frigeri, Grasselli and Krejci [14], Frigeri and Grasselli [16] and Frigeri, Grasselli and Rocca [17] replaced the chemical potential (1)4 by the following nonlocal model

μ=∫ΩJ⁡(x−y)​𝑑y​φ−∫ΩJ⁡(x−y)​φ​(y)​𝑑y+ξ​F′​(φ),\mu=\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)dy\varphi-\int_{\Omega}J(x-y)\varphi(y)dy+\xi F^{\prime}(\varphi),

obtained the nonlocal Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard equations with double-well potential or singular free energy, studied the well-posedness and long time behavior of solutions; Bosia and Gatti [6], Cherfils and Madalina [10] and You, Li and Zhang [37] investigated the properties of solutions for Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard equations with dynamic boundary conditions, studied the well-posedness and long time behavior of solutions respectively; In [38], Zhou and Fan proved the vanishing viscosity limit of solutions for the initial boundary value problem of 2D Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard equations; Giorgini, Miranville and Temam [20] studied the Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system with viscosity depending on concentration and logarithmic potential, proved uniqueness of weak solutions in 2D, and existence and uniqueness of strong solutions (global in 2D and local in 3D) with divergence free initial velocity in H01H_{0}^{1}. Liu and Shen [29], Key and Welfold [27] and Feng [15] studied the numerical approximation of solutions, etc.

There are only few results on the mathematical analysis of the Cauchy problem for incompressible Navie-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system. The first related result was obtained by Starovoitov [33]. The author supposed that FF is a suitably smooth double-well potential, studied the qualitative behavior as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty of the solutions for 2D Cauchy problem. The other paper on the Cauchy problem was written by Cao and Gal [8]. In their paper, the authors established the global retularity and uniqueness of strong/classical solutions for the Cauchy problem of 2D NS-CH equations with mixed partial viscosity and mobility. We remark that because of the difficulty caused by the convective term (the order of u⋅∇φu\cdot\nabla\varphi in (1)3 is low, one can’t control it by a fourth order linear term directly), the coupling between uu and φ\varphi (especially the term on the right hand side of (1)1) and the chemical potential, there’s no paper on the Cauchy problem of three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard equations. Thus a natural question is how to study the properties of solutions for the Cauchy problem of 3D Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard equations.

Since ±1\pm 1 can be seen as two equal minima of the double well-potential. In this paper, let ω0=±1\omega_{0}=\pm 1, we consider the global existence and the time decay rate of solutions for the following Cauchy problem:

(5) {∂tu−Δu+u⋅∇u+∇π=−Δϕ⋅∇ϕ,div​u=0,∂tϕ+u⋅∇ϕ+Δ2​ϕ=Δ⁡[(ϕ+ω0)3−ϕ],(u,ϕ)|x=0=(u0​(x),ϕ0​(x)),(x,t)∈ℝ3×ℝ+.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}u-\Delta u+u\cdot\nabla u+\nabla\pi=-\Delta\phi\cdot\nabla\phi,\\ &\hbox{div}u=0,\\ &\partial_{t}\phi+u\cdot\nabla\phi+\Delta^{2}\phi=\Delta[(\phi+\omega_{0})^{3}-\phi],\\ &(u,\phi)|_{x=0}=(u_{0}(x),\phi_{0}(x)),\end{aligned}\right.\hskip 9.24994pt(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{+}.

where ϕ=φ−ω0\phi=\varphi-\omega_{0} and ϕ0=φ0−ω0\phi_{0}=\varphi_{0}-\omega_{0}. For convenience, we rewrite (5) as

(6) {∂tu+u⋅∇u+∇π−Δu=−Δϕ⋅∇ϕ,div​u=0,∂tϕ+u⋅∇ϕ+Δ2​ϕ−Δ​ϕ=Δ⁡((ϕ+ω0)3−ϕ),(u,ϕ)|t=0=(u0​(x),ϕ0​(x)),inℝ3×(0,∞).\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla u+\nabla\pi-\Delta u=-\Delta\phi\cdot\nabla\phi,\\ &\hbox{div}u=0,\\ &\partial_{t}\phi+u\cdot\nabla\phi+\Delta^{2}\phi-\Delta\phi=\Delta((\phi+\omega_{0})^{3}-\phi),\\ &(u,\phi)|_{t=0}=(u_{0}(x),\phi_{0}(x)),\end{aligned}\right.\hskip 9.24994pt\hbox{in}~\mathbb{R}^{3}\times(0,\infty).

We note that the Laplacian operator (−Δ)δ(-\Delta)^{\delta} (δ∈ℝ\delta\in\mathbb{R}) can be defined through the Fourier transform, namely

First of all, we consider the local well-posedness of solutions for problem (6), i.e., we prove the following theorem:

Suppose that (u0,ϕ0)∈H1​(ℝ3)(u_{0},\phi_{0})\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{3}). Then, there exists a small time T~>0\tilde{T}>0 and a unique strong solution (u,ϕ)​(x,t)(u,\phi)(x,t) to system (6) satisfying

The second aim of this paper is to consider the small data global well-posedness of solutions for system (6).

Let N≥1N\geq 1, assume that (u0,ϕ0)∈HN​(ℝ3)×HN+1​(ℝ3)(u_{0},\phi_{0})\in H^{N}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\times H^{N+1}(\mathbb{R}^{3}), and there exists a constant δ0>0\delta_{0}>0 such that if

Remark 1.5.

Note that system (6) can be seen as the coupling between the Navier-Stokes equations and convective Cahn-Hilliard equation. Simple calculation shows that H˙12​(ℝ3)\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) is a critical space for 3D Navier-Stokes equations. Moreover, if v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) is a smooth solution to

(11) vt−Δ2v+∇⋅(|∇v|2∇v)=0,v_{t}-\Delta^{2}v+\nabla\cdot(|\nabla v|^{2}\nabla v)=0,

in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, then for each λ>0\lambda>0,

Hence, pp is the critical exponent if it satisfies

(12) 3p=1+k−1=k.\frac{3}{p}=1+k-1=k.

Hence, Theorem 1.4 may be seen as a small initial data global well-possedness result in the critical Sobolev space.

Hence, it is optimal.

The main difficulties to consider the Cauchy problem of 3D Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard equations are how to deal with the convective term u⋅∇ϕu\cdot\nabla\phi, the coupling between uu and ϕ\phi and the linear term of the double-well potential. Since the principle part of (6)3 is a fourth-order linear term and the convective term is only a first-order nonlinear term, due to Sobolev’s embedding L63−2​s​(ℝ3)⊂H˙s​(ℝ3)L^{\frac{6}{3-2s}}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\subset\dot{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{3}), we cannot control ‖∇kf​(ϕ)‖Lp\|\nabla^{k}f(\phi)\|_{L^{p}} through ‖∇k+2ϕ‖L2\|\nabla^{k+2}\phi\|_{L^{2}}. In order to overcome this difficulty, we borrow a second-order term from the double-well potential, rewrite (6)3 as

(17) ∂tϕ+Δ2ϕ−Δϕ=−u⋅∇ϕ+Δ[(ϕ+ω0)3−2ϕ].\partial_{t}\phi+\Delta^{2}\phi-\Delta\phi=-u\cdot\nabla\phi+\Delta\left[(\phi+\omega_{0})^{3}-2\phi\right].

Hence, one can control the convective term by the last term of the left hand side of equation (17). Moreover, in order to overcome the difficulty caused by the coupling between uu and ϕ\phi, we assume the initial data ‖(u0,∇ϕ0)‖H˙12\|(u_{0},\nabla\phi_{0})\|_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}} is sufficiently small, obtain a priori estimates on (u,∇ϕ)(u,\nabla\phi). On the other hand, we establish the suitable a priori estimates in the negative Sobolev space H˙−s\dot{H}^{-s} (0≤s≤120\leq s\leq\frac{1}{2}), obtain the optimal decay rate of strong solutions for the Cauchy problem of Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard equation in the whole spaces ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}.

The structure of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce some preliminary results, which are useful to prove our main results. Section 3 is devoted to prove the local well-posedness of solutions. In Section 4, we prove the small initial data global well-posedness of solutions in critical Sobolev space. Section 5 is devoted to study the decay rate of solutions for system (6).

3. Local well-posedness

In this section, by using Banach fixed point theorem, we prove the local well-posedness for system (6). Let

5. Decay rate

In this section, we consider the decay rate of strong solutions for system (6). First of all, we derive the evolution of the negative Sobolev norms of the solution to the Cauchy problem (6). In order to estimate the convective term and the double-well potential, we shall restrict ourselves to that s∈[0,12]s\in[0,\frac{1}{2}].

For the homogeneous Sobolev space, the following lemma holds:

Lemma 5.1.

Proof of Theorem 1.6.

Define

ℰ−s(t):=∥Λ−su(t)∥L22+∥Λ−sϕ(t)∥L22+∥Λ−s∇ϕ(t)∥L22.\mathcal{E}_{-s}(t):=\|\Lambda^{-s}u(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\Lambda^{-s}\phi(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\Lambda^{-s}\nabla\phi(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.

For inequality (60), integrating in time, by the bound (59), we have

(68) ℰ−s​(t)≤\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{-s}(t)\leq ℰ−s​(0)+C​∫0tE⁡(t)​ℰ−s​(τ)​𝑑τ\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{-s}(0)+C\int_{0}^{t}E(t)\sqrt{\mathcal{E}_{-s}(\tau)}d\tau
≤\displaystyle\leq C0​(1+sup0≤τ≤tℰ−s​(τ)​d​τ),\displaystyle C_{0}\left(1+\sup_{0\leq\tau\leq t}\sqrt{\mathcal{E}_{-s}(\tau)}d\tau\right),

which implies (13) for s∈[0,12]s\in[0,\frac{1}{2}], that is

(69) ∥Λ−su(t)∥L22+∥Λ−sϕ(t)∥L22+∥Λ−s∇ϕ(t)∥L22≤C0.\|\Lambda^{-s}u(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\Lambda^{-s}\phi(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\Lambda^{-s}\nabla\phi(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq C_{0}.

Moreover, if l=1,2,⋯,N−1l=1,2,\cdots,N-1, we may use Lemma 2.5 to have

‖Λl+1​f‖L2≥C​‖Λ−s​f‖L2−1l+s​‖Λl​f‖L21+1l+s.\|\Lambda^{l+1}f\|_{L^{2}}\geq C\|\Lambda^{-s}f\|_{L^{2}}^{-\frac{1}{l+s}}\|\Lambda^{l}f\|_{L^{2}}^{1+\frac{1}{l+s}}.

Then, by this facts and (69), we get

(70) ‖Λl+1​(u,ϕ,∇ϕ)‖L22≥C0​(‖Λl​(u,ϕ,∇ϕ)‖L22)1+1k+s.\|\Lambda^{l+1}(u,\phi,\nabla\phi)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\geq C_{0}(\|\Lambda^{l}(u,\phi,\nabla\phi)\|_{L^{2}}^{2})^{1+\frac{1}{k+s}}.

(71) dd​t​(‖Λk​u‖L22+‖Λk​ϕ‖L22+‖Λk+1​ϕ‖L22)+C0​(‖Λk​u‖L2+​‖Λk​ϕ‖L22+‖Λk+1​ϕ‖L22)1+1l+s≤0.\frac{d}{dt}(\|\Lambda^{k}u\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\Lambda^{k}\phi\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\Lambda^{k+1}\phi\|_{L^{2}}^{2})+C_{0}\left(\|\Lambda^{k}u\|_{L^{2}}^{+}\|\Lambda^{k}\phi\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\Lambda^{k+1}\phi\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\right)^{1+\frac{1}{l+s}}\leq 0.

Solving this inequality directly gives

(72) ∥Λku∥L22+∥Λkϕ∥L22+∥Λk+1ϕ∥L22≤C0(1+t)−l−s,forl=1,2,⋯,N−1,\|\Lambda^{k}u\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\Lambda^{k}\phi\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\Lambda^{k+1}\phi\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq C_{0}(1+t)^{-l-s},\hskip 9.24994pt\hbox{for}~l=1,2,\cdots,N-1,

which means (14) holds. Hence, we complete the proof of Theorem 1.6.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
